doc.title: Chuck Israels interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 11, 2021

title: Inspiration from other people's music: Skipping Tune and Walkin' Up
summary: Israels says composing starts from others' music and explains how Skipping Tune derives from Bill Evans' piece, with a brief audio dropout.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I want to go back to your composing and arranging for a bit. And can you describe where inspiration comes from? How does something new get started?
Could you give me an example?

Well I wrote a piece called “Skipping Tune.” It’s my version of Bill Evans’ piece called “Walking Up.” It is built of the same mat — no, he made a piece out of these kinds of materials, exclusively these kinds of materials. Major 7 chords, minor 7 chords and no dominants. But he did it in such a way that the piece feels as if it has progress and as if the chords have harmonic intention as if they are moving forward. They’re not static. It’s not just this chord for a while and now arbitrarily shift to this one. It has real —
I lost you for a minute. I’m still, I don’t hear you.
But yes, you were describing, in fact I heard that tune, your “Skipping Tune” and I loved the forward motion in it, and it was happy.

Yes. It is happy. There doesn’t have to be dominant chords in it. It’s interesting. You write a piece that feels as if it moves forward and doesn’t have any tritones hidden in it but it’s not really — they don’t do the same thing that a dominant chord does.
